chief_complaint: excruciating stabbing pain around left eye waking me at 2 AM every night for 3 weeks
hpi_details: 3-week history of severe, excruciating, strictly unilateral pain centered in and around his left eye and temple. Describes the pain as 'like a hot ice pick boring directly into my eyeball' (10/10 intensity). Episodes occur with clockwork regularity every single night at exactly 2:00 AM, waking him from deep sleep, and last between 45 and 60 minutes before resolving completely. During attacks, his left eye becomes bloodshot and pours with tears (lacrimation), his left nostril becomes blocked and runny, his left eyelid droops slightly, and his forehead sweats profusely. Unlike migraine sufferers who lie still in a dark room, during these attacks he experiences severe psychomotor agitation, pacing furiously around the living room unable to sit still or lie down. This is his third 'cluster period' in 4 years; previous episodes lasted 6 weeks and then vanished completely for over a year. Drinking a single beer instantly triggers a full-blown attack within 15 minutes.
ideas: thinks he has a retro-orbital sinus abscess or brain aneurysm exploding behind his eye
concerns: exhausted, driven to despair and suicidal ideation during attacks due to the sheer unendurable severity of the pain
expectations: wants immediate high-strength injectable painkiller and whatever prophylaxis can abort this cluster bout immediately
pmh: two prior identical 6-week headache clusters over past 4 years, otherwise healthy
medications: paracetamol and oral ibuprofen with zero relief
social_hx: heavy cigarette smoker (20/day since age 16), drinks alcohol socially (currently avoiding alcohol due to instant attack triggering), construction site manager

clinical_knowledge.topic: Episodic Cluster Headache evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Episodic Cluster Headache is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Immediate acute abortive therapy: 100% high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather face mask at 12 to 15 Litres/minute for 15-20 minutes (aborts attack within 15 minutes in >70% of patients; completely safe and non-sedating), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: excruciating stabbing pain around left eye waking me at 2 AM every night for 3 weeks

Key HPI features: 3-week history of severe, excruciating, strictly unilateral pain centered in and around his left eye and temple. Describes the pain as 'like a hot ice pick boring directly into my eyeball' (10/10 intensity). Episodes occur with clockwork regularity every single night at exactly 2:00 AM, waking him from deep sleep, and last between 45 and 60 minutes before resolving completely. During attacks, his left eye becomes bloodshot and pours with tears (lacrimation), his left nostril becomes blocked and runny, his left eyelid droops slightly, and his forehead sweats profusely. Unlike migraine sufferers who lie still in a dark room, during these attacks he experiences severe psychomotor agitation, pacing furiously around the living room unable to sit still or lie down. This is his third 'cluster period' in 4 years; previous episodes lasted 6 weeks and then vanished completely for over a year. Drinking a single beer instantly triggers a full-blown attack within 15 minutes.

Objective/Exam findings: Examine patient during attack or interictally. During attack: observe prominent ipsilateral cranial parasympathetic autonomic signs: left conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, forehead diaphoresis, and partial Horner's syndrome (left ptosis and miosis). Observe psychomotor agitation (pacing, rocking). Interictally: neurological exam and cranial nerves completely normal. MRI Brain (with dedicated pituitary and cavernous sinus views) to rule out structural secondary cluster-like headache (e.g., pituitary macroadenoma, cavernous sinus meningioma, or internal carotid artery dissection).
Relevant background/PMH: two prior identical 6-week headache clusters over past 4 years, otherwise healthy
Current medications: paracetamol and oral ibuprofen with zero relief
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Episodic Cluster Headache.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Migraine without aura (longer duration, prefers stillness) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Suicidal thoughts during attacks — the pain severity itself is a documented driver of suicidality and needs direct acknowledgment.
management_principles: Immediate acute abortive therapy: 100% high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather face mask at 12 to 15 Litres/minute for 15-20 minutes (aborts attack within 15 minutes in >70% of patients; completely safe and non-sedating)

Co-prescribe subcutaneous sumatriptan 6mg injection (or sumatriptan 20mg nasal spray into the contralateral nostril) for rapid abortive relief within 10 minutes (oral triptans/analgesics are too slow for short cluster attacks)

Immediate transitional bridging therapy: start short course of high-dose oral prednisolone (60mg daily tapering over 2-3 weeks) or greater occipital nerve (GON) steroid block to rapidly suppress attacks while transitional maintenance builds
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 35M male smoker presents with active cluster headache bout: nightly 2 AM strictly unilateral orbital agony lasting 45 mins, accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic features and psychomotor agitation.
reference_soap.objective: Examine patient during attack or interictally. During attack: observe prominent ipsilateral cranial parasympathetic autonomic signs: left conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, forehead diaphoresis, and partial Horner's syndrome (left ptosis and miosis). Observe psychomotor agitation (pacing, rocking). Interictally: neurological exam and cranial nerves completely normal. MRI Brain (with dedicated pituitary and cavernous sinus views) to rule out structural secondary cluster-like headache (e.g., pituitary macroadenoma, cavernous sinus meningioma, or internal carotid artery dissection).
reference_soap.assessment: Episodic Cluster Headache (Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia - TAC). DDx: Migraine without aura (differentiated by longer duration 4-72 hours, preference for lying still in dark room, absence of prominent autonomic phenomena or clockwork periodicity), Paroxysmal Hemicrania (shorter attacks 2-30 minutes occurring 10-20 times daily, 100% responsive to indomethacin), Trigeminal Neuralgia (seconds of electric shock pain triggered by touch), acute angle-closure glaucoma.
reference_soap.plan: Because he reports suicidal ideation, assess immediate safety and arrange emergency mental-health support if there is intent, a plan, or inability to stay safe. Arrange urgent clinician-led treatment of the cluster bout; high-flow oxygen and a triptan may be appropriate after contraindications are assessed. Discuss transitional and preventive treatment with a headache specialist, including ECG monitoring if verapamil is used. Advise avoiding alcohol during the active cluster bout and offer smoking-cessation support.

learning_objectives: Identify the distinguishing features of Cluster Headache (Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia): strictly unilateral orbital agony, clockwork periodicity, cranial autonomic signs, and psychomotor agitation
Explain why high-flow 100% oxygen (12-15 L/min via non-rebreather mask) and subcutaneous sumatriptan are the only effective acute abortive therapies
Prescribe high-dose verapamil as first-line preventative maintenance while executing mandatory ECG safety monitoring for PR prolongation
Formulate transitional steroid bridging therapy (oral prednisolone or occipital nerve block) to suppress bouts while verapamil takes effect

teaching.one_liner: One of the most severe pains known to medicine, striking with clockwork regularity around the same time each night, causing excruciating one-sided eye pain with tearing, nasal congestion, and restlessness — unlike migraine, sufferers pace rather than lie still.
differentials: Migraine without aura (longer duration, prefers stillness)
red_flags: Suicidal thoughts during attacks — the pain severity itself is a documented driver of suicidality and needs direct acknowledgment

must_ask.say: Does this happen at almost the exact same time every night?
Is the pain strictly around one eye, like a hot poker?
During the attack, does your eye water, your nose run, or your eyelid droop on that side?
During an attack, do you feel like pacing, rather than lying still?
Have you had bouts like this before, followed by long pain-free periods?

history.answer: Every single night around 2 AM, I wake up with this unbearable, stabbing pain behind my left eye.
It starts suddenly in my sleep and ramps up to an agonizing peak within just a couple of minutes.
This has been happening every night for the past three weeks. I had two identical six-week bouts over the last four years, but nothing in between.
It is strictly centered in and around my left eye and temple. It never affects the right side.
It feels like a red-hot ice pick boring straight into my eyeball. It is easily a ten out of ten, completely agonizing.
It wakes me up with clockwork regularity at exactly 2:00 AM, lasts 45 to 60 minutes, and then vanishes completely.
I can't lie still at all. I get intensely agitated and spend the entire hour pacing frantically around the living room.
Trying to lie down makes it feel much worse, while pacing helps me cope slightly. Nothing else really relieves it.
During each attack, my left eye turns bloodshot and tears heavily, my left nostril clogs up and runs, my eyelid droops, and my forehead sweats.
No, I don't see flashing lights, zigzag lines, or blind spots before the pain hits.
No nausea or vomiting, and I don't need a dark, quiet room like people with regular migraines do.
No, my vision stays clear and I have no double vision, aside from my eye tearing up during the attacks.
No fever, no stiffness in my neck, and no skin rash at all.
No arm or leg weakness, no numbness, no speech difficulties, and no seizures.
No, I haven't had any head injuries or accidents.
I've tried paracetamol and oral ibuprofen every night, but they provide absolutely zero relief.
Even a single sip of beer triggers an attack within 15 minutes, so I have had to stop drinking entirely.
No, I don't have high blood pressure and I don't take any blood thinners.
No one else at home is sick or having headaches, and we don't have unvented gas or charcoal heaters.
No, I have never had cancer, HIV, or taken any immune-suppressing drugs.
The pain is so excruciating and relentless that while it's happening, I feel completely desperate and have had thoughts of ending my life.
I'm terrified that I have a brain aneurysm about to burst or a severe sinus infection behind my eye.
I need an urgent fast-acting injection to stop the pain when it hits, and something to shut down this cycle for good.
Other than those two previous six-week cluster headache bouts over the past four years, I've been completely healthy.
I have never had any surgeries and I've never stayed in a hospital.
Just the over-the-counter paracetamol and ibuprofen that haven't helped. No prescription medications or supplements.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day and have been smoking since I was 16.
I usually drink socially on weekends, but I haven't touched a drop since this bout started because it instantly triggers an attack.
I work as a construction site manager and live at home with my partner.
No one in my family has a history of brain aneurysms, early strokes, or severe headaches like this.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg, heart rate is 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 36.7 C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
Alert, comfortable, sitting calmly in the chair, and in no acute distress between headache episodes.

Visual acuity and visual fields are normal bilaterally; pupils are equal, round, and briskly reactive to light; fundoscopy reveals sharp disc margins with no papilledema, and conjunctivae are clear without injection.
No tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinuses, and temporal arteries are non-tender and pulsatile bilaterally.
Neck is supple with full passive flexion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
Cranial nerves II through XII are completely intact; no ptosis, miosis, or facial asymmetry is present between attacks.
Normal muscle bulk and tone, with 5/5 strength throughout the upper and lower extremities bilaterally.
Sensation to light touch and pinprick is fully intact and symmetric across all facial divisions and body dermatomes.
Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric in all four limbs, and plantar responses are flexor bilaterally.
Finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements are smooth and accurate, gait is steady, and Romberg sign is negative.
